conceptTag: De Beers and the diamond market
readerTitle: Why De Beers stopped trying to control the diamond market
caseNote: 실제 기업 (De Beers, 사우디아라비아 석유 감산 사례) + 가상 적용 (이사 업체)
insight: 시장 가격을 떠받치는 지배 기업은 공급을 묶어 두는 비용을 혼자 낸다. 경쟁자는 그 높은 가격에 무임승차한다.
misconception: 독점력은 한 번 손에 넣으면 비용 없이 계속 이익을 낸다.

sources.text: De Beers Group, company history (1888 founding, Central Selling Organisation, 'A Diamond Is Forever' 1947)
Epstein, E. J. (1982). The Rise and Fall of Diamonds. Simon & Schuster (sights, stockpiling, Soviet marketing arrangement)
Rio Tinto announcements and press coverage of Argyle leaving the De Beers selling channel (1996)
Financial press coverage (e.g., Financial Times, Reuters) of De Beers' 2000 strategic review and 'supplier of choice' strategy
De Beers press releases on the Lightbox launch (2018) and its wind-down (2025)
Yergin, D. The Prize (Saudi Arabia as swing producer in the early-to-mid 1980s); U.S. EIA historical oil market notes

factChecks.note: De Beers의 20세기 공급 점유율은 자료마다 다릅니다(흔히 80~90%로 인용). 카드에는 수치 없이 'most of the world's rough diamonds'로만 썼습니다.
2000년 전략 전환('custodian of supply' 역할 포기, 'supplier of choice') 발표 시점과 표현을 게시 전에 1차 보도로 확인하세요.
Argyle 광산(Rio Tinto)의 CSO 이탈은 1996년, 캐나다 Ekati 광산 개장은 1998년으로 알려져 있습니다. Ekati 생산분이 'largely outside De Beers'로 판매됐다는 표현을 확인하세요.
Lightbox: 2018년 출시, 2025년 브랜드 종료 발표. 날짜와 '가격 하락이 이유'라는 설명을 De Beers 보도자료로 확인하세요. 구체적 가격 수치는 일부러 넣지 않았습니다.
사우디아라비아는 1980년대 초 반복 감산 후 1985~86년 증산으로 전환, 유가 급락. 카드에는 연도를 'early 1980s', 'mid-1980s'로만 적었습니다.
훅 카드의 '통제 비용이 커진 것이 이유 중 하나'는 재고 부담과 독립 광산 증가에 대한 일반적 보도에 근거합니다. 반독점 압력 등 다른 이유도 있었으므로 'partly'로 표현했습니다.
이사 업체 사례의 30% 저가 견적은 설명용 가상 수치입니다.

cards.title: The company that gave up control on purpose
body: For most of the 20th century, one company sold most of the world's rough diamonds: De Beers.
In 2000, it announced it would stop trying to manage the whole market. No rival had beaten it. Part of the reason was simpler: holding the market up had become very expensive.

image.label: A vault of stored diamonds behind a half-open door
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반쯤 열린 금고 안에 원석 다이아몬드가 가득 쌓여 있고, 바깥에서 작은 광부 캐릭터 몇 명이 각자 원석을 들고 지나감. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: It's the late 1990s. You're De Beers.
body: You sell most rough diamonds through one channel. When demand dips, you buy the extra stones and store them so prices don't fall.
But new mines in Australia and Canada now sell on their own, at the high price you protect. Your stockpile ties up a fortune. What do you do?

options.text: Keep buying everyone's surplus to hold the price
options.feedback: Prices stay stable, but your pile keeps growing while independent mines enjoy the price without sharing the cost.

options.text: Stop managing the whole market; sell your own stones and build your brand
options.feedback: You free up cash and stop subsidizing rivals, but you accept more price swings and a smaller share.

options.text: Release the stockpile and cut prices to squeeze the new mines
options.feedback: It could hurt rivals, but it also crushes the value of your own stones and the price you spent decades defending.

choice.afterReveal: In 2000, De Beers chose something close to B: it said it would stop acting as the custodian of world supply and aim to be the 'supplier of choice.'

cards.title: A market run from one room.
body: Cecil Rhodes merged the big South African mines into De Beers in 1888. Over the next century, most rough diamonds, including many from other producers, flowed through its selling arm in London.
Chosen buyers were invited to regular **sights** and offered a box of stones at a set price. Take it or leave it.
When demand fell, De Beers didn't cut prices. It bought the extra and stored it. When large mines opened in Soviet Siberia, it even arranged to market Soviet diamonds too.

cards.title: Monopoly power has a running cost.
body: **Monopoly power** is the ability to keep prices above what a competitive market would allow, usually by controlling supply.
But a high price tempts every producer to sell more. Someone has to hold the extra back. For De Beers, that meant a growing pile of diamonds that tied up cash and earned nothing.
Independent mines sold at the price De Beers protected without carrying any of that cost. The price maker paid. Everyone else **free-rode**.

image.label: One figure holds up a price bar while others stand under it
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 한 캐릭터가 무거운 'High price' 막대를 혼자 머리 위로 떠받치고 있고, 그 아래 그늘에서 다른 캐릭터들이 편하게 물건을 팔고 있음. 떠받치는 캐릭터 발밑에 'Stockpile' 상자가 쌓여 있음.

cards.title: How the grip loosened.
body: Each new source outside the channel made holding back supply costlier. De Beers is still a major seller today, but one of several.

breakdown.label: Rhodes forms De Beers
breakdown.detail: Big South African mines merged into one company

breakdown.label: 'A Diamond Is Forever'
breakdown.detail: Ad slogan written for De Beers to build demand

breakdown.label: Argyle leaves
breakdown.detail: Australia's big mine stops selling through De Beers

breakdown.label: Canada's first mine
breakdown.detail: Ekati opens and sells largely outside De Beers

breakdown.label: Custodian role ends
breakdown.detail: De Beers stops managing world supply

cards.title: The same trap in oil.
body: In the early 1980s, Saudi Arabia cut its own oil output again and again to support prices. Other producers kept pumping and sold at the higher price.
By the mid-1980s, Saudi Arabia gave up that role and raised output. Prices fell sharply.
The pattern repeats: when one player holds back so the whole market stays high, the others grow on its sacrifice. Sooner or later, the holder asks why it's paying.
cards.softwareNote: Software has no stockpile, but the pattern holds. A market leader that keeps prices high creates a **price umbrella** under which cheaper rivals and free alternatives grow.

cards.title: Controlling supply doesn't control substitutes.
body: De Beers also spent decades building demand, starting with 'A Diamond Is Forever.' That helped mined diamonds keep their appeal even after its supply grip weakened.
Lab-grown diamonds are a harder problem. De Beers launched its own lab-grown brand, Lightbox, in 2018 at far lower prices. In 2025 it said it would close the brand as lab-grown prices kept falling.
When a close substitute gets cheap, neither supply control nor a famous slogan fully protects your price.

image.label: A mined diamond and a lab-grown diamond on a scale
image.brief: 저울 양쪽에 거의 똑같이 생긴 다이아몬드 두 개. 왼쪽은 'Mined', 오른쪽은 'Lab-grown' 라벨, 오른쪽 가격표가 훨씬 작음. 실제 브랜드명이나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Now it's a moving company.
body: You run the biggest moving company in a mid-size city. For years, few rivals had trucks, so your rates held.
Now small crews rent trucks by the day and quote about 30% less. They win customers your high prices keep away. What do you do?

options.text: Match their prices on every job
options.feedback: You may keep share, but you cut margin on every move, including customers who would have paid more. It can start a price war.

options.text: Hold your rates and wait for the small crews to fail
options.feedback: Some will fail, but your high prices are the umbrella they grow under. You pay for the market while they take the easy jobs.

options.text: Stop defending every job; price simple moves competitively and focus on what crews can't easily copy
options.feedback: Like De Beers in 2000, you stop subsidizing rivals and put effort into insured long-distance, fragile items and office moves, where your size still matters.

cards.title: Holding a price up is a job you do for the whole market.
body: Market power lasts only while you control supply and substitutes stay weak. Until then, rivals enjoy your high price for free.
**Try it today:** list who benefits when you hold your price firm. If rivals gain more than you do, decide how long you're willing to pay for it.
